stories.headline: Schumer boasts early advantage in Senate power struggle as Dem rival warns against 'coronation'
stories.note: Senate Democrats are tearing into each other over who leads them, a messy fight that distracts from any message.
body: Senate Democrats are headed into their first contested leadership race in about 30 years, with Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland challenging Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for the right to lead the caucus as it takes the majority.

The winner needs 28 votes. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, has 15 senators publicly behind him and says he has the votes to stay on. Allies like DSCC Chair Kirsten Gillibrand credit him with delivering a 55-seat majority.

Van Hollen calls himself the underdog and has five public backers with votes, including Bernie Sanders, Jeff Merkley and progressive Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan. He claims up to 15 supporters and accused party insiders of trying to move up the Dec. 1 secret-ballot vote. "Let's not rush into a coronation," he said.

Van Hollen has gone on a cable-news blitz and launched a campaign website, complete with a donation request, arguing voters rejected the "status quo." He says he has dropped earlier thoughts of a 2028 White House run to focus on beating Schumer.

Why it matters: Instead of a unified new majority, Senate Democrats are opening with an old-guard-versus-progressive brawl, giving Republicans a divided opposition to work against for Trump's final two years.

stories.headline: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson faces audit calls after CFO quits over 'financial integrity' concerns
stories.note: A top finance official walking out over integrity concerns is a fresh black eye for one of the left's marquee big-city mayors.
body: Chicago's chief financial officer, Ashlee Gabrysch, a former Fitch Ratings executive, resigned Friday after just three months on the job, citing concerns about financial integrity, according to her resignation letter as reported by the Chicago Tribune.
Gabrysch wrote that the CFO's statements about city finances must be complete and accurate and that she could not meet those obligations under the conditions she was asked to serve in.

She had clashed with Mayor Brandon Johnson over the size of the 2027 deficit. Johnson first projected an $882 million gap, then cited a figure of $662 million after factoring in planned borrowing for police settlements. Gabrysch argued that borrowing was a temporary fix and declined to call the proposed $17.6 billion budget balanced.

Johnson's office fired back, saying she was largely absent during key budget work and accusing her of improperly directing a $75 million pension payment, a matter it said it would refer to the city's inspector general. Finance Committee chair Pat Dowell, a Democrat, called for an independent audit.

Why it matters: It is the latest in a string of departures from Johnson's finance team, including two earlier CFOs and the budget director, as the city faces credit downgrades. It hands Republicans another example of progressive big-city governance in trouble.

stories.headline: Fetterman's Gaza-born challenger calls to 'abolish ICE,' oust top Democratic leaders
stories.note: The Democrats' far-left wing keeps pushing 'abolish ICE,' a message Republicans are happy to run against in Pennsylvania.
body: Ahmed Moor, a Gaza-born member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is the first candidate to challenge Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman in the 2028 Democratic primary, he told Fox News Digital.

Moor, who grew up in Philadelphia and studied at Penn and Harvard, says the country is in a "constitutional crisis" and is running on what he calls a "Dignity Agenda" of universal healthcare, childcare and affordable housing.

He wants to abolish ICE, calling it a "paramilitary militia," while saying he would still like immigration law enforced. He also says both Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries need to be replaced as Democratic leaders.

Fetterman, who has sided with Republicans on issues like Iran, government funding and immigration, hasn't said whether he will seek a second term. He welcomed challengers and took a swipe at Moor, saying he "seems to really love Hamas."

Why it matters: The left's push to purge moderates and revive 'abolish ICE' is spreading into a must-win swing state, a fight that could leave Democrats with a nominee Republicans would love to run against.

stories.headline: Police groups condemn Mamdani over axing elite NYPD unit
stories.note: Police unions lining up against Mamdani's NYPD cuts reinforces the GOP's public-safety case against socialist Democrats.
body: New York City police unions blasted Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday after he ordered the NYPD's Strategic Response Group disbanded and replaced with new civilian-led teams to handle protests.

Under the plan announced with Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, the unit's counterterrorism duties move to an existing command, while protest response shifts to a new Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division inside the Mayor's Office of Community Safety.

Police Benevolent Association President Patrick Hendry said the mayor is putting officers and the public at risk "to appease his radical base," and warned that disruptive demonstrators now have City Hall on their side.

Detectives' Endowment Association President Scott Munro said the move shows how disconnected City Hall is from real policing. He warned detectives will be pulled off criminal cases to cover protests, pointed to the 2024 Columbia building takeover as the kind of situation the unit handled, and questioned how Mamdani's earlier civilian teams have worked out.
Why it matters: Rank-and-file police organizations openly breaking with a socialist mayor keeps public safety front and center, an issue where Republicans hold the advantage.

stories.headline: Biden library nears site decision as fundraising trails ambitions: report
stories.note: Donors aren't rushing to fund Biden's legacy project, a telling sign of how the party views his presidency.
body: Former President Joe Biden's presidential library foundation is reportedly close to picking a site in Delaware, but its fundraising is still falling short of expectations, according to filings reported by CBS News.

The foundation raised about $1.5 million in 2025 while spending $2.1 million, running a deficit of roughly $600,000. Most of the money went to staff, consultants and legal fees, including about $250,000 for consultants to build a fundraising operation. An official called 2025 a "building and infrastructure year."

This year brought two $5 million gifts, and the foundation added five board members. Some Biden allies have reportedly grumbled that Democratic donors haven't stepped up, with one source saying Biden has "never been a good fundraiser." Jill Biden is expected to help as he undergoes prostate cancer treatment.
Donor support has reportedly been strained by frustration over his presidency and his pardon of Hunter Biden. Trump's library foundation, by contrast, has already secured tens of millions of dollars.
Why it matters: Even after a big midterm year for Democratic giving, the party's donors aren't rushing to preserve Biden's legacy, a telling verdict on his presidency.

stories.headline: James Comer launches bid for Kentucky governor
stories.note: The House Oversight chairman jumping in gives Republicans a high-profile, battle-tested contender to retake the Kentucky governor's mansion.
body: House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., launched his campaign for Kentucky governor Monday night during a tele-townhall with voters.

Comer spent most of the event taking questions on education, small business and high prices, and pitched cutting Kentucky's income tax to zero to attract jobs and keep young people in the state. "Serving this state is a calling for me," he said.

The election is in November 2027, with primaries in May. Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, seen as a possible 2028 presidential contender, is term-limited. Comer narrowly lost the 2015 GOP primary to Matt Bevin but is expected to start this race as the front-runner.

In Congress since 2016, Comer has led Oversight investigations into Joe Biden's use of the autopen and the government's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case. Trump carried Kentucky by about 30 points in 2024.
Why it matters: With Beshear leaving, Republicans have a well-known, well-funded contender to take back the governor's mansion in a deep-red state.

stories.headline: Clarence Thomas calls foul on California ruling he says could turn citizens into government mouthpieces
stories.note: Justice Thomas's dissent puts California's compelled-speech DEI mandate under a spotlight, keeping conservatives' First Amendment fight alive.
body: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a challenge to California's rule requiring continuing medical education courses for doctors to include instruction on implicit bias. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented, and Justice Neil Gorsuch also would have taken the case.

The case was brought by Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, who teaches such courses, and the nonprofit Do No Harm. They argued the rule forces private instructors to deliver a government-favored message. The Ninth Circuit had ruled the courses count as government speech, putting them outside First Amendment scrutiny.
California countered that instructors don't have to endorse implicit bias and are free to say they disagree with it, and that states need broad power to set licensing requirements.

Thomas warned the ruling could let states turn private speakers into government mouthpieces. "A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny," he wrote. Do No Harm said it was disappointed but will keep fighting.
Why it matters: The denial leaves the question open, but three conservative justices flagging compelled speech signals the free-speech fight over DEI-style mandates is far from over.
